answer.summary: Noah described extending Slack’s product-market fit as a repeated, humble learning process: identify the next audience’s needs, test new levers, and adapt both the experience and product rather than assuming the old fit will carry over.

sections.heading: Treat each audience as a new product-market-fit curve
sections.content: Noah framed growth as stacking S-curves: after reaching a ceiling with one group—such as development teams in the US—Slack had to build fit again for new audiences, such as tech-savvy non-developer teams or people in large enterprises outside the US. His advice was to stay self-critical and humble, and approach the next audience with a beginner’s mindset about what it needs.

sections.heading: Research, then optimize for learning
sections.content: When Slack’s self-service fundamentals looked less healthy, the team did user research and examined cohort curves to understand how the next customers differed. Instead of continuing to optimize what had worked before, it set aside the roadmap, formed hypotheses about new levers, and tested them quickly. Noah said they accepted that the next six months—and, more broadly, the next couple of quarters—might bring little impact because the priority was learning. He reported that this process helped double the rate of new paid-customer growth in the year and the following couple of years, while accelerating self-service growth.

sections.heading: Adapt the experience and the product
sections.content: For new users beyond early adopters, Slack focused on both comprehension—whether people understood what the product was for and how it worked—and desirability—why they should care. Noah estimated the changes were roughly 60/40 between the early journey and product features. The journey was called “day one,” though it extended to about day 30 and included both individual and team experiences. Product investments included WYSIWYG message composition instead of requiring Markdown, offline mobile support, and controls for configuring sidebars and notifications so Slack would not become overwhelming as teams scaled. Noah also identified giving users a taste of the paid product through a trial as a strategy Slack had not yet figured out; the excerpt does not establish that it was implemented.

answer.summary: Weiss described extending product-market fit as repeatedly learning what a new audience needs, then adjusting the experience, product, and measures of success. Slack used research, experiments, and customer pilots to find and validate new levers rather than assuming its earlier playbook would keep working.

sections.heading: Treat each audience as a new S-curve
sections.content: Weiss framed product-market fit as stacking S-curves: win a smaller group, then find the next audience as growth from the current one approaches a ceiling. Examples included moving from developers to tech-savvy non-developer teams, or from US customers to people in large enterprises outside the US. His advice was to stay self-critical and humble, and ask what the next audience needs instead of assuming the product is permanently figured out.

sections.heading: Research, form hypotheses, and optimize for learning
sections.content: When Slack’s self-service fundamentals weakened, the team studied user research and cohort curves and recognized that newer, less sophisticated customers had different needs. Rather than keep optimizing what had worked before, they threw out the roadmap, generated hypotheses about new growth levers, and spent about six months testing which were real—even while expecting little impact during that period. Weiss said this learning-first approach later helped double the rate of new paid-customer growth and accelerate self-service.

sections.heading: Improve the new-user experience and product for the new audience
sections.content: Slack focused on whether new teams could comprehend what the product was for and why they should care. Weiss said the work was roughly 60/40 between the early journey and product features: the journey, called the “day one journey,” extended in practice to day 30 and involved both individual and team use. Changes included giving users a taste of the paid product through trials, and foundational product work such as WYSIWYG message composition, offline mobile use, and sidebar and notification controls to help Slack remain useful rather than overwhelming as teams scaled.

sections.heading: Measure team activation and validate with customers
sections.content: Slack created a “successful teams” metric: five people using Slack to communicate during the majority of the workweek. Teams reaching that threshold were 400% more likely to upgrade over the next six months. For new functionality, Slack also used a pilot program to roll features out to progressively larger customer groups and gather feedback through Slack Connect and surveys. Weiss described choosing diverse participants across industry, company size, and location who were motivated and more tolerant of the risks of beta testing; pilots could include rough features that were later killed. These methods supported repeated validation as the customer base grew more diverse.

It explains adapting the experience and product so new users can understand and get value from Slack, with examples including WYSIWYG composition, offline mobile use, and controls to prevent the product from becoming overwhelming.

answer.summary: Weiss described repeatedly re-establishing product-market fit: study the next audience, replace assumptions with testable hypotheses, prioritize learning, and adapt the experience and product to their needs. Slack reported that this approach doubled new paid-customer growth and accelerated self-service.

sections.heading: Treat each audience as a new product-market-fit challenge
sections.content: Weiss framed growth as stacking S-curves: after reaching a ceiling with one audience, identify the next audience—such as technology-savvy non-developer teams or large enterprises outside the US—and ask what they need. Stay humble and self-critical rather than assuming the product is universally solved.

sections.heading: Research, form hypotheses, and optimize for learning
sections.content: When Slack’s self-service cohort curves weakened, the team researched users and reassessed what later adopters needed. Rather than keep optimizing the old roadmap, it set that roadmap aside, generated hypotheses about new growth levers, and tested them quickly. Weiss said Slack expected to sacrifice impact for roughly six months (and the next couple of quarters) to learn which levers were real. He reported that this work doubled the rate of new paid-customer growth in the year and following years and accelerated self-service.

sections.heading: Address comprehension, desirability, and product gaps
sections.content: For newer users, Slack focused on whether they understood what the product was for and how it worked (“comprehension”), and why they should care (“desirability”). Weiss estimated the early journey accounted for about 60% versus 40% for product features, describing a team’s “day one” experience extended in practice to day 30, including both individual and team use. Slack also added foundational capabilities for the next audience, including WYSIWYG message composition, offline mobile use, and ways to configure sidebars and notifications so the product would not become overwhelming. It also developed ways to let users experience the paid product at different points in the journey.

sections.heading: Use a success signal and real-world customer feedback
sections.content: Slack introduced a “successful teams” metric: five people using Slack for communication during the majority of the work week. Teams reaching that threshold were 400% more likely to upgrade over the next six months. For ongoing validation, Slack used a pilot program to roll features out to progressively larger customer groups and gathered feedback through Slack Connect and surveys. Weiss described selecting for diversity across industry, company size, and location, and for participants motivated to help and willing to tolerate rough edges—including features that might be removed before general release.
